list-item.p: Selinexor 60 mg once weekly plus ruxolitinib was identified as the recommended phase 3 dose for treatment of patients with myelofibrosis.
Selinexor plus ruxolitinib had a suitable safety profile and promising efficacy.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The phase 1 portion of SENTRY/XPORT-MF-034 (NCT04562389) evaluated the exportin 1 inhibitor selinexor (40 mg/60 mg once weekly) plus ruxolitinib in JAK inhibitor–naïve patients with myelofibrosis (n = 24). Primary end points were maximum tolerated selinexor dose, recommended clinical trial dose, and safety. No dose-limiting toxicities were reported. Common adverse events were nausea, fatigue, anemia, thrombocytopenia, constipation, vomiting, and headache. Nausea was transient, mainly grade 1, and managed by prophylactic antiemetics. Four deaths occurred, all unrelated to study treatment. Selinexor 60 mg in combination with ruxolitinib was identified as the recommended phase 3 dose based on safety, efficacy, and exposure–response analyses. Overall safety profiles and grades of clinically significant adverse events were similar and generally manageable regardless of selinexor dose. A greater proportion of patients achieved spleen volume reduction of ≥35% (SVR35) and total symptom score reduction of ≥50% (TSS50) at week 24 in the selinexor 60-mg group (79% and 58%) than the 40-mg group (38% and 25%). Among evaluable patients who received suboptimal ruxolitinib ≤5 mg twice daily in the selinexor 60-mg group, SVR35 was observed in 100% (6/6) and TSS50 in 75% (3/4) of patients. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04562389.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Myelofibrosis (MF) is a rare hematologic malignancy associated with substantial morbidity, including splenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, fatigue, cachexia, and leukemic progression. These effects are primarily driven by oncogenic mutations in JAK2, CALR, and/or MPL in hematopoietic stem cells, resulting in mutant clonal expansion.1, 2, 3 JAK inhibitors (JAKi), the current standard of care, have demonstrated efficacy in reducing splenomegaly and symptom burden.1,4, 5, 6, 7 However, JAKi treatment is limited by modest response rates, insufficient tolerability, and limited impact on disease modification.2,8 Approximately one-third of patients treated with ruxolitinib achieve spleen volume reduction of ≥35% (SVR35) or total symptom score reduction of ≥50% (TSS50) by week 24 of treatment.2 Among SVR35 responders, the probability of maintaining response decreases as early as week 12,3 an important consideration given correlations between splenomegaly and reduced survival.9,10 Treatment-related anemia and thrombocytopenia often necessitate ruxolitinib dose interruptions and reductions, particularly to doses of ≤5 mg twice daily where long-term efficacy is not observed.4,11,12 Ruxolitinib also has a limited impact on meaningful disease modification assessed by bone marrow fibrosis, driver mutation allele burden, and anemia.3,13, 14, 15 Combination treatments have emerged to address these limitations. In the MANIFEST-2 phase 3 trial of pelabresib plus ruxolitinib and the TRANSFORM-1 phase 3 trial of navitoclax plus ruxolitinib, SVR35 at week 24 was significantly higher with combination treatment than placebo/ruxolitinib (65.9% vs 35.2%, P < .001, and 63.2% vs 31.5%, P < .0001, respectively); however, symptom responses were not significantly improved (52.3% vs 46.3%, P = .216, and 39.2% vs 41.7%, respectively) and neither combination improved anemia.16,17 Therefore, an unmet need remains for novel therapies targeting disease-relevant pathways beyond JAK/STAT alone.

Selinexor, an investigational, oral, selective exportin 1 (XPO1) inhibitor, inhibits XPO1-mediated nucleocytoplasmic cargo transport.18 In addition to modulating JAK/STAT signaling,19, 20, 21, 22 XPO1 inhibition affects non-JAK/STAT pathways, including NF-κB proinflammatory signaling,18 p53-driven cell death,22, 23, 24, 25 and cell cycle arrest.18,26,27 Nonclinical data demonstrate that XPO1-mediated nuclear export may be a critical pathway for MF pathophysiology, with XPO1 inhibition increasing malignant cell death, reducing inflammatory markers, and inducing apoptosis of JAK2-mutated MF CD34+ cells.26,28 Synergy between selinexor and ruxolitinib or other therapeutic agents in cell lines with or without JAK2V617F or TP53 mutations provides a strong rationale for further investigation of these combinations.26,28 The ongoing SENTRY phase 1/3 study is evaluating selinexor plus ruxolitinib in JAKi treatment–naïve MF; phase 1 results are presented here.

sec.title: Patients and study design
sec.p: The open-label, phase 1 portion of the multicenter phase 1/3 SENTRY (XPORT-MF-034; NCT04562389; EudraCT: 2020-003883-19) study included a 3 + 3 dose escalation followed by dose expansion (7 additional patients at 40 mg and 11 at 60 mg) (supplemental Figure 1). Preliminary safety and efficacy data across phase 1a and phase 1b informed the selection of the recommended phase 3 dose. Eligible patients were ≥18 years of age with primary or secondary MF (per 2016 World Health Organization classification of myeloproliferative neoplasms), spleen volume of ≥450 cm3, Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System intermediate-1 with ≥1 constitutional symptom (eg, anemia, fatigue, weakness, or feeling unwell) or higher,29 Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of ≤2, and platelet count of ≥100 × 109/L. Patients with >5% peripheral blood blasts or >10% bone marrow blasts or previous JAKi treatment for MF were excluded (supplemental Methods for additional exclusion criteria). The trial was approved and performed in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization, Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice, appropriate regulatory requirements, and approval of institutional review boards at enrolling institutions with principles originating from the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided a written informed consent.

sec.title: Study treatments
sec.p: Patients were assigned to receive oral selinexor 40 mg or 60 mg once weekly plus ruxolitinib twice daily (per label including dose modification per package instructions) in 28-day cycles. Selinexor dose reductions or interruptions followed protocol-defined criteria (supplemental Tables 1 and 2). If treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) required treatment discontinuation, both selinexor and ruxolitinib were to be discontinued, regardless of the drug to which the event was attributed. All patients were to receive a single-agent 5-HT3 antagonist as prophylaxis against nausea, unless otherwise contraindicated, during the first 2 cycles and optionally in subsequent cycles. A neurokinin-1 antagonist, olanzapine, or another antiemetic agent could be added if clinically indicated.

sec.title: End points and assessments
sec.p: Primary end points were maximum tolerated dose (MTD), recommended clinical trial dose, and safety. MTD was defined as the highest dose at which ≥1 of 6 patients developed dose-limiting toxicity (supplemental Methods) during cycle 1. Secondary end points included SVR35 (by magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography per International Working Group–Myeloproliferative Neoplasms Research and Treatment criteria),30 TSS50 (modified Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form version 4.0 excluding fatigue),31,32 and anemia response (International Working Group–Myeloproliferative Neoplasms Research and Treatment criteria).30 Absolute mean changes in SVR and TSS (Abs-TSS) were also assessed as exploratory end points. Duration of response was defined as the time from the first achieved SVR35/TSS50 response to the time when the patient stopped responding (SVR35, ≤35% reduction from baseline and >25% increase from nadir; TSS50, TSS equaled or exceeded the baseline value). Censoring date was defined as the last efficacy assessment date for patients who discontinued treatment or the last on-study visit date for patients still on treatment. End of treatment (EoT) was defined as treatment discontinuation, withdrawal of the patient from the study, death, or loss to follow-up, whichever occurred first. End of study was defined as completion of survival follow-up for up to 1 year after the EoT visit.

Exploratory end points included antiemetic use, weight changes, hemoglobin stabilization (hemoglobin change from baseline, ≤2 g/dL), platelet and hemoglobin levels, and efficacy by subgroups, including suboptimal ruxolitinib dosage (ruxolitinib ≤5 mg twice daily for ≥5 of the first 6 cycles). Variant allele frequency (VAF) in MF driver genes (JAK2, CALR, and MPL) and other high-molecular-risk (HMR) genes (ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1/IDH2, SRSF2, and U2AF1) were evaluated locally. Plasma cytokine and chemokine concentrations were centrally evaluated using a Luminex 200 system human cytokine/chemokine array 71-plex panel (Eve Technologies, Calgary, Canada). Transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) and hepcidin were evaluated using the Millipore TGF-β 3-Plex Discovery Assay (MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA) and the R&D Human Hepcidin enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN), respectively. Bone marrow biopsies were obtained at screening and week 24. Slide pairs were stained centrally for reticulin, CD61, and CD71. Independent digital images of stained bone marrow slides were evaluated to calculate megakaryocyte density (mean number of CD61+ cells from ≤10 randomly selected fields per image) and spatial analysis (mean distance between nuclei in a field with variable number of nuclei/field and ≤10 fields per image), percentage of CD71+ erythroid cells, and area of reticulin fibers (mean number of intersections from ≤10 randomly selected 400 mm2 fields per image).33,34

sec.title: PK
sec.p: Exposure–response analyses were conducted using model-derived pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters (from empirical Bayes estimates) used to generate exposure models aligned with observed data for both selinexor and ruxolitinib, and association with efficacy and selected safety end points was explored. Ruxolitinib steady-state concentrations were categorized as low or high based on median exposure.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Safety and efficacy were analyzed using data cutoffs of 24 February 2023 (primary completion) and 1 August 2023 (duration of response and updated safety). Analyses included all patients who received ≥1 dose of study treatment. The efficacy-evaluable population consisted of all patients who had ≥1 dose of study drug treatment and baseline and postbaseline (12 or 24 weeks) spleen imaging or TSS evaluation, respectively. The primary TSS50 analysis population included all enrolled patients who had a nonzero baseline TSS. Nonresponder imputation was used for missing data.

sec.title: Patients, disposition, and drug exposure
sec.p: Between June 2021 and August 2022, 24 patients were enrolled and received ≥1 dose of selinexor (40 mg or 60 mg) plus ruxolitinib (Table 1; supplemental Figure 2). Patients were predominantly male (67%) and had a median age of 64 years (range, 44-77), and 46% had primary MF. The Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System risk category was intermediate-1 in 29% (7/24), intermediate-2 in 46% (11/24), and high risk in 25% of patients (6/24). Five patients had received previous antineoplastic medications (supplemental Table 3). Median platelet count was 257.5 × 109/L (range, 101.0-746.0) and median hemoglobin was 10.0 g/dL (range, 7-14.6 g/dL). Driver mutations at baseline were JAK2 (75%; 18/24), CALR (21%; 5/24), and MPL (4%; 1/24), with concomitant HMR mutations in 46% of patients (11/24). Median baseline spleen volume was 1655 cm3 (650-3657). Median baseline TSS (excluding fatigue) was 16 (0-54).

sec.p: As of 24 February 2023, the median duration of exposure to selinexor plus ruxolitinib was 31.5 weeks (range, 6-68) (supplemental Table 4); 13 patients discontinued treatment and 18 patients remained on study (supplemental Figure 2). Reasons for treatment discontinuation were TEAEs (40-mg group: 20%, 2/10; 60-mg group: 21%, 3/14), physician decision (60-mg group: 14%, 2/14), patient withdrawal (40-mg group: 20%, 2/10; 60-mg group: 7%, 1/14), progressive disease (acute myeloid leukemia; 60-mg group: 7%, 1/14), and other (40-mg group: 10%, 1/10; 60-mg group: 7%, 1/14). Two patients (60-mg group) discontinued the study and study drug to receive allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Four deaths occurred during the study, 2 (both in the 60-mg group) within 30 days of final drug administration (1 owing to leukemic transformation [accelerated phase/blast phase progression, cause of death acute myeloid leukemia]; 1 owing to uncertain cause suspected by investigator to be related to underlying chronic heart failure with fluid overload and ascites) and two >30 days after last dose (40-mg, unknown cause; 60-mg, posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder). None of the deaths were considered related to the study drug by the study investigators.

sec.title: Dose-limiting toxicities
sec.p: Three patients were enrolled at each dosage (40 mg once weekly and 60 mg once weekly) in phase 1a. No dose-limiting toxicities were reported.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All 24 patients experienced ≥1 TEAE, 17 of 24 (71%) experienced ≥1 grade 3+ TEAE, and 8 of 24 (33%) experienced serious TEAEs (Table 2). Common TEAEs overall were nausea (18/24; 75%), fatigue (14/24; 58%), anemia (13/24; 54%), thrombocytopenia (13/24; 54%), constipation (9/24; 38%), vomiting (9/24; 38%), and headache (9/24; 38%). Neutropenia was reported in 7 of 24 (29%) patients and leukopenia in 6 of 24 (25%). Although numerically higher in the 60-mg dose group, overall safety profiles and grades of clinically significant TEAEs were similar between dose groups.

sec.p: To further support the manageability of the safety profile, exploratory analyses were performed to determine potential mitigating effects of antiemetic prophylaxis. Nausea events among all patients were predominantly grade 1 (50%) and transient in nature (median duration, ∼2 cycles); 1 patient had grade 3 nausea but had not received antiemetic prophylaxis. Among patients who received ≥1 prophylactic antiemetic (58% of all patients), nausea (grade 1 only in the 60-mg group, 1 grade 2 in the 40-mg group) was experienced by 64% of patients compared with 90% of those not receiving prophylactic antiemetics (grades 1-3). Despite the incidence of nausea, over the 10 treatment cycles, absolute weight increased (median increase of 2.5 kg at week 28 in the 60-mg group; supplemental Figure 3).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: SVR and symptom improvements observed at week 12 were sustained to week 24, with numerically higher response rates in the 60-mg group (Table 3; Figure 1A-B). SVR35 was achieved at week 24 in 11 of 14 (79%) patients in the 60-mg group and 4 of 10 (40%) in the 40-mg group; most patients in the 60-mg group (10/14; 71%) achieved SVR35 at week 12 compared with 3 of 10 (30%) in the 40-mg group. All patients in the efficacy-evaluable population in the 60-mg group achieved SVR35 at any time (supplemental Figure 4A). Mean (standard deviation) absolute change in spleen volume from baseline at week 24 was −1201 cm3 (592) in the 60-mg group and −433 cm3 (223) in the 40-mg group.

sec.p: TSS50 was achieved at week 24 by 7 of 12 (58%) patients in the 60-mg group and by 4 of 10 (40%) in the 40-mg group. In the efficacy-evaluable population, 9 of 10 (90%) patients treated with selinexor 60 mg and 8 of 10 (80%) treated with 40 mg achieved TSS50 at any time (supplemental Figure 4B). Both SVR35 and TSS50 were achieved at week 24 in 6 of 12 (50%) patients treated with 60 mg and at any time in 9 of 12 (75%) patients (Figure 1C). Improvements in symptom scores were observed across all domains by week 12 for both groups (Figure 1D). Mean (standard deviation) absolute changes from baseline in TSS were −19 (13) for the 60-mg group and −8 (8) for the 40-mg group in the efficacy-evaluable population. After the maximum 78-week follow-up, the probability estimate of maintaining SVR (median follow-up, 32 weeks) and TSS50 (median follow-up, 51 weeks) in the 60-mg group was 100% (supplemental Figure 5; additional information on TEAEs, patient disposition, and dose exposure at the 1 August 2023 cutoff can be found in supplemental Tables 5-7).

There were no differences for SVR35 and TSS50 across key subgroups, and responses were independent of baseline hemoglobin or platelet levels (Figure 2). No differences were found between subgroups who received ruxolitinib 5/10 mg twice daily vs 15/20 mg twice daily (Figure 2). Seven patients received selinexor plus suboptimal ruxolitinib dose (≤5 mg twice daily for ≥5 of the first 6 cycles); of these patients, 6 of 7 (86%) achieved SVR35, and 5 of 7 (71%) achieved TSS50 at any time (Figure 3). All patients receiving suboptimal ruxolitinib in the 60-mg group achieved SVR35 at any time.

sec.title: Hemoglobin and platelet change
sec.p: Anemia response (≥2 g/dL increase in hemoglobin level in patients with baseline hemoglobin <10 g/dL) was achieved at any time in 2 patients (1 in each dose group); 6 of 13 patients (46%) in the 60-mg group and 5 of 10 (50%) in the 40-mg group achieved hemoglobin stabilization. Median hemoglobin levels remained stable through the 10 treatment cycles (Figure 4A). Median platelet counts initially decreased in the 60-mg group and then stabilized at >100×103/μL throughout the study; platelet counts in the 40-mg group remained consistently at >100×103/μL (Figure 4B).

sec.title: Exploratory biomarkers
sec.p: Baseline and post-treatment VAFs were available for 13 patients. Mutations were observed across all 3 driver genes, with mutations in JAK2 in 9 patients, CALR in 3 patients, and MPL in 1 patient (supplemental Figure 6). Reduction in VAF at week 24 was observed in 6 of 8 evaluable patients (75%) in the 60-mg group and in 5 of 5 (100%) in the 40-mg group. Reduction in VAF of ≥20% was observed in 4 of 13 patients (31%); 2 patients with the highest VAF reduction at week 24 (∼30%) were also characterized to have ≥50% VAF at baseline and to be at HMR of ASXL1 and IDH2 mutations. SVR35 was achieved at any time in 11 of 13 patients (85%) with available VAF values.

At baseline, 76% of the 75 cytokines and chemokines analyzed were elevated in MF samples compared with healthy donor samples (data not shown). In most patients (pooled data), early decreases in proinflammatory MF-relevant cytokines were observed by week 4 and maintained at least until EoT (supplemental Figure 7). Affected cytokines included TGF-β1, interferon ɣ, tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin-7 (IL-7), IL-1RA, and IL-16. Early reductions (week 4) in some cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, IL-1RA, IL-7, TGF-β1, and IL-18, were associated with week 24 SVR (supplemental Figure 8). Patients in the 60-mg group were generally characterized by a greater, although not statistically significant, reduction in cytokine plasma levels compared with the 40-mg group.

Bone marrow biopsy pairs were available from 14 patients (4 from the 40-mg group; 10 from the 60-mg group). At screening, 1 sample was grade MF-0, 3 were MF-1, 5 were MF-2, 3 were MF-3, and 2 were undetermined. Local MF grade was available for 11 patients, with poor concordance between centrally and locally reviewed data sets; the patient graded MF-0 centrally was graded MF-2 by local review, and only 1 of the 3 patients graded MF-1 centrally was similarly graded locally. In this small cohort of patients, there was no correlation between baseline JAK2V617F VAF and baseline bone marrow MF grade. Based on the central pathologist review of reticulin-stained slides, MF grade was stable at week 24 in most patients, and only 2 worsened (1 from MF-1 to MF-2, 1 from MF-0 to MF-3). However, whole-slide analysis of 8 pairs (screening and week 24) of biopsies showed decreased reticulin fiber density in 3 patients (37%), decreased CD61+ megakaryocytic progenitor density in 3 (37%) patients, increased megakaryocyte nuclei distance in 4 (50%) patients, and increased CD71+ erythroid progenitors in 2 (25%) patients.

sec.title: PK
sec.p: Noncompartmental analysis results are presented in supplemental Table 8. There was a clear trend of increasing exposure with increasing dose for both selinexor and ruxolitinib (supplemental Figure 9). Simulations using population PK models suggested no impact of ruxolitinib on selinexor exposure or vice versa (data not shown). Patients with model-derived week 1 area under the concentration–time curve (AUCW1) of >2500 h × ng/mL had a 100% (9/9) response rate for SVR35 at any point in the study, whereas patients with an AUCW1 of <2500 h × ng/mL had an SVR35 of 56% (5/9) (supplemental Figure 10). Based on a population PK model simulation, ∼30% of patients achieved the AUCW1 target of 2500 h × ng/mL with 40 mg once weekly, and ∼80% achieved this target with 60 mg once weekly. Overall mean ruxolitinib steady-state concentration for all patients was 225nM (134nM in the AUCW1 of <2500 h × ng/mL group and 326nM in the AUCW1 >2500 h × ng/mL group; supplemental Figure 11). Given the ruxolitinib exposures observed, the SVR35 response rate in this study was higher than expected with ruxolitinib alone based on historical exposure–response analysis,35 particularly in patients with exposures of ≤185nM (7/10 responders; 70%), with a 30% expected response rate (3/10). There was no clear exposure–response relationship with selinexor exposure for safety end points (data not shown).

sec.title: Recommended phase 3 dose
sec.p: Selinexor at 60 mg once weekly in combination with ruxolitinib offered a manageable safety profile and a substantially improved clinical benefit over the 40-mg dose, which was further supported by the clinical pharmacology analysis. Thus, 60 mg once weekly in combination with ruxolitinib was identified as the recommended phase 3 dosage.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This phase 1 component of SENTRY evaluated safety and tolerability of selinexor plus ruxolitinib in JAKi-naïve patients with MF. No dose-limiting toxicities were identified, and thus, no MTD was determined. Notably, 60 mg once weekly was selected as the recommended phase 3 dosage based on substantially higher efficacy (SVR35 at week 24 of 79% vs 40%) without meaningful differences in safety profiles, supported by PK exposure–response analyses.

Overall, selinexor plus ruxolitinib demonstrated a generally tolerable safety profile without major end-organ toxicities. Most TEAEs were grade 1/2, nonserious, and managed with supportive care or dose modifications. Common TEAEs were anemia, nausea, fatigue, thrombocytopenia, constipation, vomiting, and headache with no apparent safety trends when comparing dose levels, acknowledging small numbers and possible confounding effects of ruxolitinib and disease status. Nausea and vomiting rates were consistent with the known selinexor toxicity profile, potentially owing to centrally induced nausea and vomiting after crossing the blood-brain barrier. Meaningful weight gain was observed, suggesting no detrimental effect of nausea on patient weight. Previous experience with selinexor in multiple myeloma has shown a direct correlation between selinexor dose and nausea,36 which tends to be limited to the first 2 cycles, with improvement as tolerance develops.37 For patients who received recommended single prophylactic antiemetics, nausea and vomiting were transient and limited to grade 1. Retrospective analyses have shown no apparent superiority in efficacy for any agent/antiemetic class on selinexor-related nausea and have shown that dual antiemetic prophylaxis is superior to single antiemetic prophylaxis, with substantially lower rates of grade 3+ nausea and vomiting.38,39 Accordingly, dual antiemetic prophylaxis is mandated for the first 2 cycles of SENTRY phase 3.40

Thrombocytopenia and neutropenia were generally asymptomatic laboratory abnormalities without clinical sequelae. Initial platelet and hemoglobin decreases, similar to those reported for ruxolitinib monotherapy,10,32 increased again before stabilizing around week 8, suggesting no clear detrimental or even potentially beneficial effect of selinexor. The patient who discontinued treatment owing to progressive disease had increasing blast counts before study drug initiation, so acute myeloid leukemia transformation was likely unrelated to treatment.

Splenomegaly is associated with worsening of disease symptoms and, although not included in prognostic scores, may decrease survival and limit treatment outcomes.41, 42, 43 Selinexor 60 mg plus ruxolitinib resulted in rapid, deep, and sustained SVR and robust symptom improvement. Symptom reductions were observed across all TSS domains, including fatigue, which has the greatest impact on patient quality of life.44,45 SVR35 or TSS50 rates in the 60-mg group exceeded those expected with JAKi monotherapy,2 although no direct comparison with other trials can be drawn. The exposure–response analysis provides strong support for SVR35 response rates beyond what would be expected with ruxolitinib monotherapy based on historical exposure–response analysis,35 particularly in patients with below-average ruxolitinib exposures (≤185 nM), where 70% of patients achieved SVR35 compared with an expected response rate of 30%. SVR35 and TSS50 responses at low or reduced ruxolitinib doses commonly used in clinical practice in response to reduced platelet counts or anemia46, 47, 48 have been reported as limited,49,50 and responses have not been observed with long-term maintenance at 5 mg twice daily.4 In patients receiving selinexor plus suboptimal ruxolitinib doses, spleen and symptom responses were maintained, with 86% of patients achieving SVR35 and 71% achieving TSS50 at any time. This evidence for the efficacy of selinexor in the absence of an effective ruxolitinib dose may indicate a fundamental role of XPO1 in MF pathogenesis. Two studies are investigating the potential for selinexor monotherapy in patients with MF: ESSENTIAL (NCT03627403) in patients refractory or intolerant to JAKi51 and the currently ongoing and recruiting SENTRY-2 (XPORT-MF-044; NCT05980806) in JAKi-naïve patients with MF and moderate thrombocytopenia.52

In nonclinical studies, selinexor selectively induced apoptosis in malignant MF CD34+ cells and inhibited CD34+ cell proliferation through p53-dependent and p53-independent pathways.27 Underscoring the potential of selinexor to act in synergy with multiple therapeutic agents, depletion of malignant cells is more pronounced when combined with ruxolitinib or other MF therapeutic agents than when either drug is used alone.27 Reductions of VAF seen in the current trial, a feature not typically observed with ruxolitinib alone,2 align with selective targeting of malignant clones,26 possibly through antiproliferative activity of nuclear accumulation of proapoptotic p53 in affected cells.53 Although higher JAK2 VAF is sometimes associated with more advanced fibrosis,54 reductions in VAF do not consistently translate into immediate or concordant histopathologic improvement, and bone marrow fibrosis changes may not parallel clinical responses after JAKi therapy in MF.55 In addition, NF-κB transcriptional activity is inhibited by selinexor-induced nuclear localization of IκBα that is enhanced by the ruxolitinib combination.28,56 Changes in cytokine levels showed correlative trends with week 24 SVR, supporting the hypothesis that XPO1 inhibition decreases NF-κB activity and synthesis of specific cytokines.18 NF-κB, a central transcriptional regulator of inflammation, has a fundamental role in MF pathogenesis, contributing to both symptoms and proliferation of malignant MF clones.8,54 Although the exploratory analysis of biomarkers affecting biological MF hallmarks was suggestive of disease modification, this preliminary proof of concept will need to be corroborated by a longitudinal evaluation in a larger cohort of patients.

The SVR observed with selinexor plus ruxolitinib compares favorably with that seen with ruxolitinib monotherapy in recent studies, with more than doubling of SVR35 at week 24.10,57 These results are comparable with those of navitoclax plus ruxolitinib and pelabresib plus ruxolitinib, with more favorable TSS50 responses in response to selinexor.17,58 Although these differences may be caused in part by the exclusion of intermediate-1-risk MF from the COMFORT studies, resulting in a higher-risk patient population compared with SENTRY phase 1, MANIFEST-2 and TRANSFORM-1 also evaluated treatment-naïve patients and included patients with intermediate-1-risk MF. Limited real-world evidence has demonstrated that ruxolitinib monotherapy achieves SVR35 in ∼27% to 55% of patients with intermediate-1-risk MF at 6 months, which is still numerically less than the SVR35 shown with the combination of selinexor plus ruxolitinib in the present phase 1 study.59,60 Despite the rates of nausea and vomiting in SENTRY phase 1, there was still a reduction in Abs-TSS, which is important, given that chronic patient-based symptoms and clinical side effects are key considerations in oral long-term frontline settings. Thus, the SENTRY phase 3 study, in which 1 goal is to demonstrate long-term tolerability of an all-oral combination, will include Abs-TSS as a coprimary end point and requires a dual antiemetic for the first 2 cycles to help manage time-limited nausea symptoms.

In conclusion, this study provided proof of concept for XPO1 inhibition with selinexor plus ruxolitinib as a treatment strategy in MF. Selinexor plus ruxolitinib exhibited a suitable safety profile without adverse impact on hematologic parameters and with promising clinical activity associated with changes in biomarkers suggestive of disease modification, a feature not observed with ruxolitinib monotherapy. Selinexor’s multifaceted mechanism of action could synergize with ruxolitinib efficacy in the context of a heterogeneous disease such as MF. Selinexor 60 mg once weekly was selected for the phase 3 portion of this study to further evaluate this all-oral combination as a potential first-line treatment for JAKi-naïve patients with MF.
